mittelalter#sections.3.paragraphs.2: Technical innovations changed everyday life and warfare: the mechanical clock, invented around 1300, divided the day into hours of equal length for the first time and struck from the towers of the cities. Papermaking, which came from China by way of the Arabs, as well as spectacles, the stirrup, and the crossbow spread, and around 1320 the first cannon appeared in Europe. In the Andes the Inca built terraced fields, suspension bridges, and a road network of more than 30,000 kilometres without iron or the wheel, on which runners carried messages and supplies.
islamische-welt#summary: Out of the message of Muhammad an empire arose within a century that reached from Spain to India, and whose scholars in Baghdad, Córdoba, and Cairo brought science, medicine, and philosophy to a new flowering.
islamische-welt#overview.0: Around 610 Muhammad, a merchant from Mecca, began to proclaim to his fellow men revelations that, according to Islamic belief, he had received from God. His message of the one God, of social justice, and of the Last Judgement met with resistance in Mecca, so that in 622 he emigrated to Medina. There the first Muslim community arose; with this emigration, the Hijra, the Islamic calendar begins. By his death in 632 most of the tribes of Arabia had joined Islam.
islamische-welt#overview.1: Under the first caliphs, Arab armies conquered Syria, Palestine, Egypt, Persia, and North Africa in an astonishingly short time. From 661 the Umayyads ruled from Damascus over an empire that by 711 also included Spain and parts of Central Asia; their expansion westwards was halted in 732 at Tours and Poitiers. Christians and Jews lived as protected subjects under Islamic rule; they paid a special tax but were allowed to keep their religion.
islamische-welt#overview.2: In 750 the Abbasids replaced the Umayyads and in 762 founded Baghdad, which soon became the largest city in the world. Under caliphs such as Harun al-Rashid and al-Ma'mun, science flourished in the House of Wisdom: Greek, Persian, and Indian works were translated into Arabic, and scholars such as al-Khwarizmi, al-Razi, and Ibn Sina laid the foundations of algebra, astronomy, and medicine. The Muslims adopted the numerals with zero from India and papermaking from China.
islamische-welt#overview.3: Politically the caliphate fell apart: in Spain the Umayyads proclaimed a caliphate of their own in Córdoba in 929, in Egypt the Fatimids ruled, and Turkish sultans took power in the East. From 1096 the Crusades brought war with the Europeans; Saladin reconquered Jerusalem in 1187. In 1258 the Mongols destroyed Baghdad and put an end to the caliphate of the Abbasids.
islamische-welt#overview.4: Despite this catastrophe the Islamic world remained a connected cultural sphere in which travellers such as Ibn Battuta encountered fellow believers, mosques, and Arabic-speaking scholars everywhere from Morocco to China. Trade across the Sahara, the Indian Ocean, and the Silk Road spread Islam as far as West Africa, India, and Indonesia. Around 1300 the empire of the Ottomans arose in Anatolia, which conquered Constantinople in 1453 and became the new great power.
islamische-welt#consequences.0: Islam became a world religion with almost two billion believers today and shapes the culture, law, and everyday life from Morocco to Indonesia.
islamische-welt#consequences.1: Arab scholars preserved and extended the knowledge of antiquity; through translations from Toledo and Sicily, algebra, medicine, astronomy, and the philosophy of Aristotle reached Europe.
islamische-welt#consequences.2: The Arabic numerals adopted from India, paper, and numerous words such as algebra, sugar, coffee, or cipher are part of the European heritage.
islamische-welt#consequences.3: Muslim trade networks connected three continents and carried goods, plants such as sugar cane and oranges, and techniques such as irrigation and windmills over vast areas.
islamische-welt#consequences.4: The conflicts of the Crusades and the conquest of Constantinople shaped the relationship between Europe and the Islamic world up to the present day.
islamische-welt#keyFacts.0: In 624 the young Muslim community wins its first victory at Badr; in 680 the death of Husayn at Karbala deepens the separation of Sunnis and Shiites.
islamische-welt#keyFacts.1: From 717 to 718 the great Arab siege of Constantinople fails; in 750 the Abbasid revolution overthrows the Umayyads.
islamische-welt#keyFacts.2: Around 820 al-Khwarizmi founds algebra in Baghdad with his book on calculation; in 859 Fatima al-Fihri endows the al-Qarawiyyin mosque in Fez, one of the oldest institutions of higher learning in the world.
islamische-welt#keyFacts.3: In 969 the Fatimids found Cairo and in 970 the al-Azhar mosque, which still exists today as a place of learning.
islamische-welt#keyFacts.4: In 1071 the Seljuks defeat Byzantium at Manzikert and open Anatolia to Turkish settlers.
islamische-welt#keyFacts.5: In the 12th century Ibn Rushd expounds the works of Aristotle in Córdoba and thereby shapes the thinking of the European universities; in the 14th century Timbuktu and the Alhambra become emblems of Islamic scholarship and art.
islamische-welt#keyFacts.6: From 1370 to 1405 Timur conquers an empire from Delhi to Ankara; in 1492 the fall of Granada ends almost 800 years of Muslim rule in Spain.
islamische-welt#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
islamische-welt#sections.0.paragraphs.0: After Muhammad's death in 632, four caliphs from his closest circle took over the leadership of the community; Muslims call them the rightly guided caliphs. Even in this period the dispute over the legitimate succession broke out: the followers of Ali, the cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet, regarded the leadership as a matter for his family, while the majority held the election of the most suitable man to be right. Out of this conflict the Shiites and the Sunnis emerged, and the struggles from 656 to 661 as well as the death of Husayn at Karbala in 680 became founding narratives of both branches.
islamische-welt#sections.0.paragraphs.1: The caliphs of the Umayyads and the Abbasids understood themselves as successors of the Prophet with religious and worldly authority, but in fact governed with administrations shaped by Persian practice, with viziers, tax registers, and postal routes. From the 9th century onwards provinces broke away under dynasties of their own: the Aghlabids and Fatimids in North Africa, the Samanids and Buyids in Persia, the Umayyads in Spain. The caliph in Baghdad remained a spiritual head whose name was mentioned in the Friday prayer, while Turkish military slaves and later the Seljuks exercised actual power.
islamische-welt#sections.0.paragraphs.2: From the 11th century the sultan, the holder of power in the name of the caliph, became the typical ruling figure of the Islamic world. The Seljuks, the Ayyubids of Saladin, the Mamluks in Egypt, and finally the Ottomans relied on cavalry armies, military slaves, and the revenues from land that they granted to their officers. Conquerors such as the Mongols and Timur destroyed cities and irrigation systems, but soon adopted Islam themselves and supported scholars and master builders at their courts.
islamische-welt#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
islamische-welt#sections.1.paragraphs.0: The cities were the heart of the Islamic world: around the Friday mosque lay the bazaar with its lanes arranged by trade, the caravanserai for merchants, baths, fountains, and residential quarters with inner courtyards. Cairo, Baghdad, Damascus, and Córdoba were among the largest cities of their time, supplied by irrigated fields, granaries, and a network of long-distance roads. In the countryside peasants lived in villages under landlords, alongside nomads who bred camels, sheep, and horses and who protected caravans or raided them.
islamische-welt#sections.1.paragraphs.1: Religion shaped the course of the day with five prayers, the fasting month of Ramadan, the prohibition of wine and pork, and the alms tax for the poor. Christians, Jews, and Zoroastrians lived as protected subjects with their own communities, courts, and houses of worship, but had to pay a poll tax and were mostly excluded from high office; in al-Andalus and Baghdad Jewish physicians, viziers, and scholars nevertheless rose to prominence. Slavery was widespread; slaves from Africa, the Caucasus, and the steppes served in households, armies, and palaces, and military slaves such as the Mamluks could rise as far as rulership.
islamische-welt#sections.1.paragraphs.2: Women were legally disadvantaged, but received shares of inheritance, could own property, and could establish endowments. Aisha, the wife of the Prophet, transmitted hundreds of sayings of Muhammad and taught in Medina, Fatima al-Fihri endowed a mosque with a college in Fez, and rulers such as Shajar al-Durr in Egypt or Raziyya in Delhi governed in their own right for a time. In poems, travel accounts, and legal documents women appear as merchants, poets, mystics, and scholars.
islamische-welt#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
islamische-welt#sections.2.paragraphs.0: In the 8th and 9th centuries the foundations of the Islamic religious sciences were laid: scholars collected and examined the hadiths, the transmitted sayings of the Prophet, and developed four Sunni schools of law from them. Alongside legal scholarship, the mysticism of Sufism flourished, which strove for immediate experience of God; Rabia of Basra, al-Ghazali, and Rumi joined it with poetry and philosophy, and Sufi brotherhoods carried Islam to India, Anatolia, and Africa.
islamische-welt#sections.2.paragraphs.1: The translation movement of Baghdad laid the ground for centuries of original research. Al-Khwarizmi created algebra, al-Biruni calculated the radius of the earth, Ibn al-Haytham founded optics on experiments, al-Razi and Ibn Sina wrote medical textbooks, and observatories were built in Maragha and Samarkand. Philosophers such as al-Farabi and Ibn Rushd interpreted Aristotle anew; from the 13th century their Latin translations from Toledo determined the curriculum of the universities from Paris to Padua. In the 14th century Ibn Khaldun devised a theory of the rise and fall of empires that is regarded as the beginning of the social sciences.
islamische-welt#sections.2.paragraphs.2: Because pictorial representations were avoided in mosques, artists brought calligraphy, geometric ornament, and the arabesque to the highest perfection. Mosques with domes, minarets, and prayer niches, palace cities such as the Alhambra, manuscripts of the Quran, miniature painting from Persia, and carpets from Anatolia show the variety of the art. Poetry was the most esteemed art; the Persian epics of Ferdowsi, the quatrains of Omar Khayyam, and the love poetry of Hafez are still read today.
islamische-welt#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
islamische-welt#sections.3.paragraphs.0: The Islamic world lay at the intersection of the trade routes of three continents. Caravans brought gold and slaves from West Africa across the Sahara to North Africa, ships sailed with the monsoon from Basra and Aden to India, East Africa, and China, and the Silk Road connected Baghdad by way of Samarkand with the Far East. A common language, Islamic law, and the gold dinar made business over thousands of kilometres easier; merchants used bills of exchange, credit, and trading companies long before these became customary in Italy.
islamische-welt#sections.3.paragraphs.1: Agriculture and technology were advanced by the farmers and engineers of the Near East: water wheels, underground channels, and cisterns irrigated fields from Persia to Spain, where rice, sugar cane, cotton, oranges, and lemons were grown. From the 8th century paper mills were established in Samarkand and Baghdad and made libraries, administration, and the book trade possible. Scholars such as al-Jazari described pumps, water clocks, and automata, and from Damascus and Toledo came famous blades, glassware, and ceramics.
islamische-welt#sections.3.paragraphs.2: The wealth of the cities depended on safe trade routes and intact irrigation systems. The devastation wrought by the Mongols in the 13th century and by Timur in the 14th, the plague from 1347, and the shift of trade to the sea routes of the Europeans from 1500 hit the old centres hard. At the same time new areas flourished: Timbuktu and Gao on the Niger, Kilwa and Zanzibar on the East African coast, Malacca in Southeast Asia, and the rising Ottoman Empire with Bursa and later Istanbul.
asiatische-grossreiche#summary: From Genghis Khan's Mongol Empire to the heyday of the Qing, great empires dominated Asia: the Ming and Qing in China, the Mughals in India, the Safavids in Persia, Joseon in Korea and the Tokugawa in Japan created stable orders, magnificent capitals and economies that long outstripped Europe's.
asiatische-grossreiche#overview.0: In the early 13th century Genghis Khan united the steppe peoples of Mongolia and launched a wave of conquest without parallel. His sons and grandsons subjugated northern China, Central Asia, Persia and the Russian principalities, destroyed Baghdad in 1258 and in 1241 advanced as far as Silesia and Hungary. The Mongol Empire became the largest contiguous land empire in history. After the destruction of many cities there followed a period, known as the Pax Mongolica, in which merchants, envoys and missionaries could travel under Mongol protection from Persia to China.
asiatische-grossreiche#overview.1: The world empire soon broke up into successor states: Kublai Khan's Yuan dynasty in China, the Ilkhanate in Persia, the Chagatai Khanate in Central Asia and the Golden Horde on the Volga. In 1368 the peasant's son Zhu Yuanzhang drove the Mongols out of China and founded the Ming dynasty, which built a new capital at Beijing, sent fleets under Zheng He as far as East Africa and expanded the Great Wall into its present form. In the west, Timur built a short-lived empire around 1400 whose heirs promoted art and science in Samarkand. The Golden Horde continued to dominate the Russian principalities into the 15th century, until Moscow finally stopped paying tribute in 1480.
asiatische-grossreiche#overview.2: In India the Delhi Sultanate ruled from 1206, and in the south the Hindu empire of Vijayanagara. In 1526 Babur, a descendant of Timur, founded the Mughal Empire, which under Akbar, Shah Jahan and Aurangzeb came to cover almost the entire subcontinent and produced buildings such as the Taj Mahal. In Persia, Shah Ismail I made the Shia branch of Islam the state religion from 1501; under Abbas I, Isfahan became one of the most splendid cities in the world. The Mughals and Safavids long fought over Kandahar but shared a common Persian court culture in which Persian served as the language of administration and poetry.
asiatische-grossreiche#overview.3: In East Asia long-lasting orders took shape. In Korea the Joseon dynasty ruled from 1392, and its king Sejong created an alphabet of its own. After repelling the Mongols in 1274 and 1281, Japan went through a century of civil wars until Oda Nobunaga, Toyotomi Hideyoshi and Tokugawa Ieyasu unified the country. From 1639 the Tokugawa shogunate restricted contacts with the outside world and secured peace for more than two centuries. In Southeast Asia, Ayutthaya, Malacca and the Vietnamese state of Đại Việt rose, while the Khmer empire of Angkor lost its dominance.
asiatische-grossreiche#overview.4: In 1644 the Manchus took Beijing and founded the Qing dynasty, which under the Kangxi and Qianlong emperors extended its territory to Taiwan, Mongolia, Tibet and Xinjiang. At the same time Russian Cossacks and fur traders pushed across Siberia to the Pacific, so that in 1689 Russia and China agreed on a border by treaty for the first time. Around 1800 China and India were still the largest economies in the world; but the Mughal Empire was already disintegrating, the British had established themselves in Bengal, and the rejection of Macartney's British embassy in 1793 foreshadowed the conflicts of the 19th century.
asiatische-grossreiche#consequences.0: For a time the Mongols linked Asia and Europe into a single space of trade and exchange; along these routes knowledge, goods and techniques such as gunpowder and paper money reached the West, but in the 14th century so did the plague.
asiatische-grossreiche#consequences.1: China's present-day borders largely go back to the conquests of the Qing, and Beijing has remained the capital almost continuously since the Ming period.
asiatische-grossreiche#consequences.2: The Mughal Empire and the Safavids shaped the language, architecture and religion of South Asia and Iran to this day: Urdu, the Taj Mahal and Iran's Shia character are legacies of this era.
asiatische-grossreiche#consequences.3: The Korean alphabet Hangeul and the Edo culture of Japan with haiku, kabuki and woodblock prints are part of humanity's cultural heritage; Isfahan's Royal Square and the Forbidden City in Beijing are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
asiatische-grossreiche#consequences.4: Russia's expansion into Siberia made it a Eurasian great power with a long border with China.
asiatische-grossreiche#consequences.5: Japan's seclusion and China's self-confident rejection of European trade demands determined the course of the encounter with the West in the 19th century.
asiatische-grossreiche#keyFacts.0: In 1206 Temüjin is proclaimed Genghis Khan; in the same year the Delhi Sultanate emerges in northern India.
asiatische-grossreiche#keyFacts.1: In 1271 Kublai Khan proclaims the Yuan dynasty; in 1274 and 1281 his fleets fail off Japan.
asiatische-grossreiche#keyFacts.2: In 1368 Zhu Yuanzhang founds the Ming dynasty; from 1405 to 1433 Zheng He's fleets sail as far as East Africa.
asiatische-grossreiche#keyFacts.3: In 1446 King Sejong of Korea promulgates the Hangeul alphabet.
asiatische-grossreiche#keyFacts.4: In 1501 Ismail I founds the Safavid Empire, and in 1526 Babur founds the Mughal Empire with his victory at Panipat.
asiatische-grossreiche#keyFacts.5: In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu wins at Sekigahara; from 1639 Japan largely closes itself off from the outside world.
asiatische-grossreiche#keyFacts.6: In 1644 the Manchus take Beijing; in 1689 Russia and China fix their border in the Treaty of Nerchinsk.
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.0.title: Rule and Politics
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.0.paragr: Mongol power rested on an army organized in units of ten, a hundred, a thousand and ten thousand warriors, on fast mounted archers and on a network of relay stations. Conquest was carried out with great severity: cities that resisted were often destroyed completely, while those that submitted paid tribute and kept their rulers. The successor states soon adapted to the societies they had conquered: the Yuan governed China with Chinese officials, while the Ilkhans and the Golden Horde adopted Islam. The principle that only descendants of Genghis Khan could be recognized as khans remained influential into the early modern period.

The great empires of the following centuries were monarchies headed by a ruler who justified his power in religious terms. The Chinese emperor was regarded as the Son of Heaven holding the Mandate of Heaven, while the Great Mughal and the shah combined Islamic ideas of rule with Persian and Central Asian traditions. The Safavids relied at first on the Qizilbash, Turkmen cavalry warriors, and the Mughals on a system of ranks into which they integrated both Muslims and Hindu Rajputs. The Qing ruled as a Manchu minority through their Eight Banners while also adopting the Chinese civil service examination.

In Japan real power lay not with the emperor in Kyoto but with a supreme military commander, the shogun. After centuries of changing shogunates and the civil wars of the Sengoku period, the Tokugawa created a lasting order: some 250 lords, the daimyō, had to reside in Edo in alternate years and leave their families there. Korea under Joseon and Vietnam under the Lê dynasty adopted Chinese models of administration and formally recognized the Chinese emperor as overlord within the tribute system, yet remained independent. States such as Ayutthaya and Malacca drew their power above all from trade.
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.1.title: Society and Everyday Life
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.1.paragr: In all the Asian empires the great majority of people lived as farmers in villages, growing rice, wheat, millet or cotton. Their taxes in money, grain or labour service paid for palaces, armies and officials. Famines, floods and wars hit them especially hard; the fall of both the Yuan and the Ming dynasties began with peasant uprisings. From the 16th century China's population grew strongly, helped by new crops from the Americas such as maize and sweet potatoes, and reached about 300 million people around 1800.

Societies were strictly hierarchical. In China the scholar-officials enjoyed the highest prestige, in Japan under the Tokugawa the samurai stood above farmers, artisans and merchants, and in Korea the yangban formed a hereditary upper class. In India castes and religious communities shaped the coexistence of Hindus, Muslims, Sikhs and Jains. At the same time great cities such as Beijing, Delhi, Isfahan and Edo – the last of which had around a million inhabitants in the 18th century – grew up with markets, theatres and teahouses.

Women usually lived under the guardianship of fathers and husbands; in China foot-binding spread, and in India noblewomen were kept in seclusion. Nevertheless, individual women wielded great influence. Sorghaghtani Beki, Kublai Khan's mother, helped steer the politics of the Mongol Empire, Nur Jahan effectively ruled the Mughal Empire alongside her husband, and court ladies, merchant women and poets in Korea and Japan left letters, diaries and poems. Shah Jahan's love for his late wife Mumtaz Mahal was turned into architecture in the Taj Mahal.
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.2.title: Culture, Religion and Knowledge
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.2.paragr: Asia's religions continued to spread and change during this period. Through merchants and Sufis, Islam reached India, Malacca and the islands of Indonesia, while Theravada Buddhism became the dominant religion in Siam, Burma and Cambodia. In Persia the Safavids made Twelver Shiism the state religion, and in China, Korea and Japan Neo-Confucianism shaped state and family. In the Punjab the Sikh religion arose around 1500 with Guru Nanak, and Akbar had representatives of different faiths debate with one another at his court.

Scholars and rulers promoted science and learning. Ulugh Beg had an observatory built in Samarkand whose star catalogue was among the most accurate before the invention of the telescope. In Korea the oldest surviving book printed with movable metal type was produced in 1377, and King Sejong had an easy-to-learn script developed as well as rain gauges and water clocks. The Ming emperors had huge encyclopedias compiled, and the Qing a collection of more than 3,000 works that also served to censor unwelcome writings.

Art and architecture reached high points. Mughal art combined Persian, Central Asian and Indian elements in miniatures and in buildings such as the Taj Mahal and the Red Fort in Delhi. Isfahan, with its great square and its mosques covered in blue tiles, became the epitome of Persian art, and the Forbidden City the epitome of Chinese palace architecture. In Japan the tea ceremony and Nō theatre developed, and later, in the cities of the Edo period, kabuki, puppet theatre, haiku poetry and the colour woodblock print.
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.3.title: Economy and Technology
asiatische-grossreiche#sections.3.paragr: During these centuries Asia was the economic centre of gravity of the world. China and India produced large quantities of silk, porcelain, tea and cotton cloth that were in demand from East Africa to Europe. Under the Pax Mongolica trade on the Silk Road flourished, and the Mongol relay system linked Beijing with Tabriz and the Volga. The Yuan government issued paper money, which European travellers such as Marco Polo described with astonishment.

Maritime trade across the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea connected ports such as Calicut, Malacca, Ayutthaya, Guangzhou and Nagasaki. Muslim, Chinese, Indian and Malay merchants used the monsoon winds for regular voyages. At the beginning of the 15th century Zheng He's Ming fleets showed what technical capabilities China possessed, but afterwards the court restricted private maritime trade. From the 16th century large quantities of silver flowed from the Americas and Japan into China, where taxes were increasingly paid in silver.

Technologically, the Asian empires had mastered irrigation, canal building, porcelain making and metal casting to a high standard; the Grand Canal supplied Beijing with grain from the south. Gunpowder weapons, invented in China, became a decisive instrument of power for the Mughals, the Safavids and the Japanese lords in the form of cannon and muskets. Russian fur traders opened up Siberia for the sake of valuable sable pelts. Around 1800 the balance began to shift as European trading companies became territorial powers, above all in India.
osmanisches-reich#summary: From a small principality in northwestern Anatolia grew a world empire that lasted more than six centuries and from 1453 ruled southeastern Europe, the Middle East and North Africa from Istanbul and gave many peoples and religions a common roof.
osmanisches-reich#overview.0: Around 1300 Osman I founded one of many Turkish principalities in northwestern Anatolia, on the border with the weakened Byzantine Empire. His successors conquered Bursa in 1326, crossed into Europe in 1354 and made Edirne their second capital. With the victory at Kosovo in 1389 Serbia became a tributary, and by the end of the 14th century the Ottomans ruled large parts of the Balkans. The defeat by Timur near Ankara in 1402 plunged the young empire into a war between brothers, but it recovered within a decade.
osmanisches-reich#overview.1: In 1453 Mehmed II conquered Constantinople and, as Istanbul, made the city the capital of an empire that saw itself as the heir of Rome and the leading power of the Islamic world. Selim I defeated the Persian Safavids in 1514 and the Mamluks in 1516/17; with that, Syria, Egypt and the holy places of Mecca and Medina passed to the Ottomans. Under Suleiman the Magnificent the empire reached the height of its power: after the victory at Mohács in 1526 he conquered large parts of Hungary, besieged Vienna in 1529 and had administration and law reorganized.
osmanisches-reich#overview.2: The empire rested on a distinctive order: the sultan ruled with a grand vizier and a council, cavalrymen received the revenues of land in return for military service, and the Janissaries, recruited through the levy of boys, formed the first standing infantry in Europe. Christians and Jews lived in religious communities of their own that largely governed themselves. In the 17th century court factions, sultans' mothers such as Kösem and powerful grand viziers gained influence, and the empire held its ground despite crises until the failed siege of Vienna in 1683.
osmanisches-reich#overview.3: With the Treaty of Karlowitz in 1699 the retreat from central Europe began, and in the 18th century Russia became the most dangerous adversary; the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 cost the empire control over the Crimea. Sultans such as Selim III and Mahmud II tried to counter the decline with reforms; Mahmud dissolved the Janissaries in 1826. The Edict of Gülhane in 1839 began the Tanzimat era, in which law, administration, schools and army were rebuilt on European models and all subjects were to be made equal before the law. In 1876 the empire received a constitution; as early as 1878, however, Sultan Abdülhamid II prorogued parliament indefinitely.
osmanisches-reich#overview.4: In the 19th century Greece, Serbia, Romania and Bulgaria broke away from the empire, which European diplomats called the "sick man of Europe"; in 1875 the state was bankrupt. The Young Turks forced a return to the constitution in 1908, but lost almost all European territories in the Balkan Wars of 1912/13. In the First World War, fought on Germany's side, their government committed the genocide of the Armenians. After the defeat of 1918 the Allies occupied Istanbul; the national movement under Mustafa Kemal abolished the sultanate in 1922, and in 1923 the Republic of Turkey was founded.
osmanisches-reich#consequences.0: The borders and nation states of southeastern Europe and the Middle East emerged to a great extent from the break-up of the Ottoman Empire; many conflicts from Bosnia to Palestine have their roots here.
osmanisches-reich#consequences.1: Istanbul, Edirne, Sarajevo, Cairo and Damascus still bear the stamp of Ottoman mosques, bazaars, baths and bridges, above all the buildings of the architect Sinan.
osmanisches-reich#consequences.2: Coffeehouses, tulips, yogurt, carpets and Janissary music travelled from the Ottoman Empire to Europe and shaped everyday life, fashion and music there.
osmanisches-reich#consequences.3: The coexistence of Muslims, Christians and Jews in self-governing religious communities is still discussed today as an example of premodern toleration, but also of legal inequality.
osmanisches-reich#consequences.4: The Tanzimat reforms and the constitution of 1876 were early attempts at modernization in the Islamic world, on which the Republic of Turkey and other successor states built.
osmanisches-reich#consequences.5: The violence of the final decades, especially the Armenian Genocide and the expulsions in the Balkans, shapes the culture of remembrance in the region to the present day.
osmanisches-reich#keyFacts.0: In 1326 Orhan conquers Bursa and makes the city the first capital of the Ottomans.
osmanisches-reich#keyFacts.1: In 1389 the Ottomans win at Kosovo; in 1402 Bayezid I is defeated by the conqueror Timur near Ankara.
osmanisches-reich#keyFacts.2: In 1453 Mehmed II conquers Constantinople, which as Istanbul becomes the capital of the empire.
osmanisches-reich#keyFacts.3: In 1517 Selim I conquers Egypt; in 1526 Suleiman the Magnificent wins at Mohács and in 1529 besieges Vienna.
